ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Plant based proteins are green, sustainable, and renewable materials that show the potential to replace traditional formaldehyde resin. High performance plywood adhesives exhibit high water resistance, strength, toughness, and desirable mildew resistance. Adding petrochemical-based crosslinkers is not economically viable or environmentally benign; this chemical crosslinking strategy makes the imparted high strength and toughness less attractive. Herein, a green approach based on natural organic-inorganic hybrid structure enhancement is proposed. The design of soybean meal-dialdehyde chitosan-amine modified halloysite nanotubes (SM-DACS-HNTs@N) adhesive with desirable strength and toughness enhanced by covalent bonding (Schiff base) crosslinking and toughened by surface-modified nanofillers is demonstrated. Consequently, the prepared adhesive showed a wet shear strength of 1.53 MPa and work of debonding of 389.7 mJ, which increased by 146.8 % and 276.5 %, respectively, due to the cross-linking effect of organic DACS and toughening effect of inorganic HNTs@N. The introduction of DACS and Schiff base generation enhanced the antimicrobial property of the adhesive and increased the mold resistance of the adhesive and plywood. In addition, the adhesive has good economic benefits. This research creates new opportunities for developing biomass composites with desirable performance.

ce:section.ce:para: Vegetable protein adhesives based on agricultural processing by-products have the advantages of environmental protection, low cost, sustainability, and degradability, which have attracted much attention in recent years [1–3]. Soy protein (SP) is considered as one of the most promising alternatives for aldehyde-based adhesives [4–6]. However, traditional SP adhesives are less suitable for plywood production. Compared with aldehyde-based adhesives, unmodified SP adhesives' wet strength is lower and insufficient for production [7]. In addition, SP protein adhesives are generally rich in protein, polysaccharides, and other nutrients, resulting in a limited storage life [8]. The cured adhesive is also susceptible to microbial attack in humid environments, reducing the useful life of plywood. A series of enhancement strategies have been developed to improve the wet adhesion properties of SM-based adhesives to meet industrial production and application needs, such as tuning protein molecules to increase surface groups [9], filling (1D/2D)nanomaterials [10–12], enhancing cross-linked networks [13,14], and biomimetic enhancement strategy [4,15]. The modulation of protein molecules was achieved by altering the spherical structural unfolding of protein through the addition of protease [16], sonication [17], acid treatment, alkali treatment, microwave treatment [18], and the addition of surfactant to expose more hydrophobic/hydrophilic ends and improve the water resistance of the adhesive, which enhancement was usually limited. The addition of 2D nanosheets, represented by graphene and boron nitride, was proven to enhance the strength of SM adhesive, but the complex exfoliation process and surface modification made the preparation process cumbersome [19]. The bionic SM adhesive, inspired by the underwater adhesion of mussel/barnacle/octopus sucker, showed great water resistance, but the high cost of preparation was prohibitive for man-made panel industry applications [18,20]. The simple molecular regulation has not improved the anti-mold performance of the adhesive, and the extensive use of complex synthetic materials increased the adhesive cost [21]. The increase in cross-linked networks in the past usually involved the use of large amounts of cross-linking agents to increase strength, which certainly increased the brittleness of the cross-linked network and was detrimental to the toughness of the adhesive [22]. In addition, the crosslinkers usually used in industry relied on non-renewable petrochemicals, which ran counter to green and sustainable development strategies [23]. It remains challenging to design a SP-based adhesive with high strength, high toughness, water-resistant and long storage time at low cost.

Organic-inorganic combinations, especially polymer-inorganic hybrid materials, which combine the benefits of both organic and inorganic phases, have been applied to develop applications for enhancing material properties, especially mechanical property [24–26]. For instance, organic-inorganic composite strategies have been used in medicine [27], biology [28], hydrogels [29], composite films [30], etc. However, composite structures with improved mechanical properties, beneficial antibacterial activity, and mildew resistance have not been seen. Chitosan (CS) is a structural polysaccharide, a product of deacetylation of chitin, and the second most abundant compound in nature. CS is a linear copolymer of β-(1 → 4) linked 2-amino-2-deoxy-β-d-glucopyranose and 2-amino-2-deoxy-β-d-glucopyranose repeating elements. It has good biocompatibility, biodegradability, non-toxicity, high bioavailability, simple modification, and antibacterial properties [31,32]. However, the low solubility under neutral and alkaline conditions limits its application range. Periodate oxidation of polysaccharides has received extensive attention [33,34], and was first used to prepare the corresponding dialdehyde polysaccharides from cellulose [35], starch [36], and sodium alginate [37]. The periodate oxidation of CS is relatively less studied and applied. The chain flexibility and solubility of CS were significantly improved with the periodate oxidation. In addition, the oxidation process confers multiple functional aldehyde groups to CS. The aldehyde groups (-CHO) within the double aldehyde CS (DACS) have the opportunity to react with the free amino groups within the SM, as demonstrated by glyoxal [38].

Halloysite nanotubes (HNTs) are a kind of convoluted layered silica-aluminate clay that are abundant and inexpensive [39]. The molecular formula of HNTs is Al2(Si2O5) OH4-nH2O with a large specific surface area and nanotubular structure [40–42]. The inner surface of HNTs is composed of Al–OH and the outer surface is composed of SiO, and this structural feature can be easily used for surface modification, such as silane modification [43]. This can help to improve the interfacial binding ability and dispersibility of HNTs clay in polymers. Compared to montmorillonite and kaolinite, HNTs have the advantage that no exfoliation is required. Therefore, the benefits and biocompatibility of HNTs are significantly improved compared to nano-fillers of conventional composites.

This work aims to develop an eco-friendly SM-based adhesive with desirable strength, toughness, and mold resistance by building a natural organic-inorganic hybrid structure combined with a Schiff base reaction and new energy dissipation mechanism. Compared to previous work, the newly prepared SM adhesive in this study has higher mildew resistance time, less cost, and chemical addition, which is expected to replace the use of commercial SM-crosslinkers. The natural organic structure DACS enhanced the cohesion of the adhesive by Schiff base interaction and hydrogen bonding, promoting its mechanical strength and water resistance. The natural inorganic structure HNTs@N interspersed in the cross-linked network of the adhesive by Schiff base action imparted desirable toughness to the adhesive by inducing stress concentration (Fig. 1 ). The prepared adhesive showed strong resistance to mildew with good antimicrobial property of DACS and Schiff base, which prolonged the adhesive and plywood service life. Compared to phenolic formaldehyde (PF) resin and commercially available SM-based adhesives, SM-DACS-HNTs@N showed cost benefits. This study provided a viable solution to create natural plant protein materials with desirable water resistance, strength, toughness, mold resistance, and economy.

SM (53 % protein content) was supplied by Yuwang Ecological Food Industry Co. CS (deacetylation >90 %, 100 < viscosity <200 mPa s), sodium periodate (AR), sodium hydroxide (AR), acetic acid, anhydrous sodium acetate (AR), hydrochloric acid (38 %), and 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APTES, AR) were supplied from Shanghai Maclean Biochemical Technology Co. HNTs were provided by Xi'an Mogina Instrument Manufacturing Co. The epoxy cross-linking agent, triglycidylamine (TGA) was prepared in the laboratory. Dialysis bag was supplied by Hunan Yibo Biotechnology Co.

DACS was synthesized by a three-step process. Firstly, CS (1 g) was dissolved uniformly in 70 mL of acetate solution at pH = 4.5 by mechanical stirring. Sodium periodate (1.328 g) was dissolved uniformly in 20 mL of deionized water and slowly added to the CS solution. The above experimental device was placed in a light-proof environment, and the reaction was terminated by magnetic stirring in an ice bath for 48 h. Residual sodium periodate was eliminated by adding 10 mL of ethylene glycol and stirring for 2 h. The impurities were removed by vacuum filtration and the mixed solution was transferred to a dialysis strip (MWCO 500) and dialyzed 4 times (24 h each time) in deionized water. The completed analyte was freeze-dried in an ultra-low temperature refrigerator for 24 h. Finally, the obtained yellow flocculent DACS was quickly sealed in a sealed bag and dried for backup.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Preparation of amino functionalized halloysite nanotubes
ce:section.ce:para: The amine functionalization of APTES was achieved by referring to the scheme of Yuan et al. [72], with some adjustments to the synthesis process. First, APTES (1.5 mL) was dissolved evenly in 50 mL of ethanol. Purified HNTs (3 g) was added to a three-neck flask and sonicated for 1 h. The suspension was refluxed under constant stirring at 80 °C for 24 h. A drying tube containing granulated calcium chloride was connected to the end of the reflux system. The ethanol was recovered by centrifugation at 5000 ppm for 10 min. The resulting solid was washed thoroughly three times with fresh ethanol to remove excess APTES, and then dried at 120 °C for 12 h to obtain HNTs@N.

TGA was synthesized as previously reported by Jeanne et al. [44]. The synthesis of TGA was completely void of petrochemical resources. Epichlorohydrin and ammonia were mixed in a molar ratio of 5:1. The reaction was carried out at room temperature by mechanical stirring for 24 h, then continued at 60 °C for 2 h and finally cooled to 20 °C. Excess NaOH (50 wt%) was added and stirred for another 2 h. The residual epichlorohydrin and ammonium hydroxide were removed by vacuum distillation to obtain TGA.

The SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive was prepared as follows: A mixture of SM, different amounts of DACS, and TGA were evenly dissolved in deionized water and stirred for 10 min. The HNTs@N was evenly dissolved in deionized water under the same conditions. The above solutions were evenly mixed to prepare the SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive. The adhesive used as a control was formulated following the procedures described above. The formulations of SM-based adhesives are shown in Table 1 .

ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization of CS, DACS, and SM-based adhesives
ce:section.ce:para: The FTIR spectra of CS, DACS, HNTs, HNTs@N, and SM-based adhesives were recorded by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, Nicolet 6700) over the scanned wavelength range of 500 to 4000 cm−1. CS and DACS were characterized via 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H NMR, 400 MHz, Bruker Biospin, Switzerland). The grafting rate of APTES in HNTs and thermal stability of CS, DACS and SM-based adhesives were measured by a TGA50 analyzer (TA Instruments, USA). The X-ray diffraction spectra of samples were measured by a multifunctional X-ray diffractometer (Ultima IV) with a scanning range of 10–80° and 5–65° with a scanning speed of 10°/min. The microstructures of HNTs and HNTs@N were detected using a transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Hitachi HT-770, Japan). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) data of the samples were recorded by Thermo Scientific™ K-Alpha™ (USA) with Al Kα radiation. The fracture morphology of the cured adhesives was photographed with a Phenom XL scanning electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Science Instrument, USA, 10 kV).

Three-layer plywood samples were prepared as follows: adjacent veneers were assembled vertically in the grain direction by applying 180 g/m2 of liquid adhesive to the surface of individual veneers. The plywood was hot pressed at 120 °C and 1.0 MPa for a pressing time of 330 s. After that, the resulting plywood was left at room temperature for 24 h. The plywood was sawn to the dimensions described in Scheme 1 . The dry shear strength was tested on a universal tensile testing machine at a 10 mm/min loading rate. In particular, the specimens used to determine the wet shear strength were soaked at 63 °C for 3 h in advance. The wood breakage rate of plywood specimens was tested according to the Chinese National Standard GB/T 18259-2018 and the Forestry Industry Standard of the People's Republic of China LY/T 2720-2016. It was visually estimated by testing the percentage of the glued wood fiber or torn part of the shear area of the specimen on the shear damage surface. The wood breakage rate of the adhesive was an average of three plywood specimens.

The residual rate and hygroscopicity were determined by the weight change of the adhesive: the sample was dried in an oven at 120 °C to a constant mass (m0), the sample was wrapped in filter paper, soaked in water at 63 °C for 6 h, and then dried at 120 °C to a constant weight (m1). The 200-mesh adhesive powder sample was dried at 120 °C to a constant weight (M0) and then placed in a container (40 °C, relative humidity 90 %). The weight of the adhesive sample was recorded every 30 min until constant weight (M1).

The different formulations of SM-based adhesives (12 g) were placed evenly in Petri dishes and stored in sealed bags (relative humidity of about 85 %). The surface of the adhesive layer was observed for mold and possible odor changes every 24 h at room temperature. Also, the mold behavior was also observed by placing the fresh liquid adhesive in a closed environment at 30 °C and 95 % relative humidity. Especially, the anti-mildew property of the adhesive was evaluated by the change in wet shear strength: different formulations of adhesives were placed at room temperature and their wet shear strength was measured every 12 h. The adhesive samples were placed in tinfoil shells and dried at 120 °C for 3 h. The tinfoil shells were placed in a desiccating dish containing a saturated salt solution and the desiccating plate was placed in an oven at 40 °C to observe the mold behavior of the cured adhesives. In addition, different formulations of five-ply plywood were prepared with SM-based adhesives and commercially available urea-formaldehyde resin adhesives. Afterward, the plywood was sawn into 100 × 25 mm specimens using a circular sawing machine. The specimens were then placed in the above-mentioned dry dishes to observe the moldy condition of the plywood.

Previously, sodium periodate-mediated polysaccharide oxidation was widely investigated. However, natural polysaccharides were mainly diol-based, including starch, cellulose, sodium alginate, and plasmonic acid [45,46]. It was observed that such oxidation could occur when the hydroxyl group was replaced by primary ammonia [47]. The oxidation reaction product, water-soluble bis-formal CS, brings plenty of binding sites for the reinforcement of the composite. Additionally, the oxidation of CS by sodium periodate would open the pyranoside ring, thereby enhancing the flexibility of the molecular chain.

The periodate oxidation of CS was shown in Scheme 2 . The FTIR spectra were used to demonstrate the structure of CS (Fig. 2a). The spectral band near 3430 cm−1 in the CS infrared spectral curve was attributed to the stretching vibrations of OH and NH. The CH stretching absorption peaks of methyl and hypomethyl groups were found around 2930 cm−1. The absorption peaks attributed to amide I (CO stretching) and amide II (NH bending and CN stretching) appeared at 1660 and 1560 cm−1. The peaks at 1579 and 1060 cm−1 on the CS disappeared completely after oxidation, indicating that the pyranoside ring of the polysaccharide was opened. Most importantly, the characteristic absorption peak of the faint aldehyde group at 1778 cm−1 appeared, which could confirm the successful preparation of DACS [47,48]. 1H NMR spectra were used to further demonstrate the formation of DACS (Fig. 2b). The signals of the polysaccharide at 3.0–3.1 ppm were dramatically decreased, suggesting the oxidative breakage of the CC bonds and the formation of the bialdehyde units [49].

XRD was used to characterize the crystallization properties of CS and DACS (Fig. 2c). The XRD pattern of CS showed a weak peak at 11.2° and a strongly diffracted peak at 20°. In the DACS curve, the diffraction peak at 11.2°disappeared completely, and the diffraction peak at 20° revealed a dramatically reduced conversion to a broader and weaker peak. This was attributed to the opening of the pyran ring of CS after oxidation, which weakened the hydrogen bonding between CS molecules and disrupted the crystalline form of CS [47].

High-resolution XPS analysis of C1 s was performed to further explain the internal interactions of CS and DACS (Fig. 2d-e). The binding energy of CN shifted from 285.78 eV to 285.84 eV and the peak area decreased from 46.23 % to 31.15 %, mainly because the oxidation of periodate reduced the number of amino groups, which gave the molecule a higher binding energy [50,51]. In addition, the peak area of CO increased from 22.97 % to 38.85 %, which further proved the successful preparation of DACS. The thermal properties of CS and DACS were characterized by TG and DTG (Fig. 2f). Two apparent stages of weight loss were observed in the CS curve [52]. The first stage at 30–120 °C was attributed to the loss of water from the sample. The main decomposition stage was observed in the range of 180–370 °C, which corresponded to the degradation of CS polymer chains and the breaking of covalent bonds, etc. The TG curves of DACS showed similar two thermolysis stages. Importantly, the DTG curve of DACS demonstrated a lower maximum degradation rate than CS. This is due to the lower molecular weight of CS oxidation products and the poorer stability of the aldehyde group. A similar situation was shown in the studies on starch and cellulose oxidation with sodium periodate.

HNTs generally exhibit weaker binding through weaker interactions with guest molecules (consisting mainly of hydrogen bonds or van der Waals forces). Fortunately, selective functionalization of their external interfaces can be easily achieved, Contributing to the enhanced binding capacity of pristine nanotubes. Fig. 3a shows the surface and crystal structures of the nanotubes. HNTs were grafted to APTES via the surface –OH and the internal –OH exposed by the surface breakage. The TEM image confirmed the broken structure of HNTs (Fig. 3b). In addition, HNTs@N exhibited a rough surface compared to HNTs. This was attributed to the attachment of APTES. The FTIR spectra of the samples before and after modification were recorded to analyze the potential radical changes (Fig. 3c). In the HNTs spectrum, the stretching vibration peaks of Al–OH appeared at 3720 and 3650 cm−1, and the deformation vibration peak of Al–O–Si appeared at 536 cm−1. For HNTs@N spectrum, the characteristic peak at 2930 cm−1 was attributed to the –CH2 asymmetric stretching and the peak at 1490 cm−1 was attributed to the –NH2 vibration [53]. In addition, the –OH at 3450 cm−1 vibrational peak tends to become stronger, which might be caused by the overlap with the stretching vibrational peak of –NH2. These suggested that the APTEs were successfully grafted onto the HNTs.

XPS full scan spectra further confirmed the occurrence of the reaction (Fig. 3d). The peak values of Al, Si, and O were observed at the binding energy of 73, 102, and 530 eV, respectively, which were the constituent elements of HNTs. The detection of N and C was observed at 398 and 285 eV on HNTs@N, which indicated the successful loading of APTES onto the nanotubes [54]. The XRD spectra of HNTs before and after the modification were shown in Fig. 3e. The HNTs with 2θ = 21.8°−26.6° showed strong characteristic diffraction peaks, and the characteristic peaks at 2θ = 12.2° corresponded to the interlayer spacing of the structure units of halloysite nanotube [55], which was 0.72 nm. The XRD spectra of HNTs@N showed the same peaks compared to HNTs, which indicated that the HNTs@N structural unit remained unchanged, and APTES were not intercalated between the layers of the elosite nanotube structural unit. Therefore, it was inferred that APTES might react with HNTs tube-end –OH, Al–OH inside the tube, or –OH appeared on the outer surface due to defects. The thermolytic properties of HNTs and HNTs@N were evaluated by TG and DTG (Fig. 3f). Two noticeable mass losses appeared in the TG curve of HNTs, the weight loss between 30 and 400 °C was attributed to the loss of physiosorbed water and residual water between the nanotube layers. Larger losses were observed between 400 and 550 °C, which was related to the decomposition of Al–OH in the structure of HNTs. HNTs@N demonstrated more weight loss, which was attributed to the decomposition of organosilane functional groups, laterally verifying the successful grafting of APTEs onto HNTs. The degree of substitution (DS) can be calculated from the weight loss rate [54]. DS (%) = (Weight loss of HNTs@N − Weight loss of HNTs) / (1 − Weight loss of HNTs) × 100 %. The calculated DS of HNTs@N was 1.76 %.

To gain insight into the composition of modified adhesives and the possible reactions that may occur, high resolution XPS C 1s and N 1s spectra were examined (Fig. 4a. For the pure SM adhesive, the peaks at 283.7, 285.2, and 287.6 eV were designated as CC, CO, COH, and CO fractions, respectively. The addition of CS caused no noticeable change. Obviously, the addition of DACS caused an additional peak at 285.6 eV. This was attributed to CN, proving that the –CHO of DACS reacted with the –NH2 of SM via Schiff base reaction [56,57].The CN bonds in the C1s spectrum of SM-DACS-HNTs@N appeared at the 285.8 eV, which was related to the fact that the addition of HNTs@N brought a large amount of –NH2 that can be effectively combined. N 1s spectrum also provided important evidence to produce Schiff bases in adhesive. The N 1s curve of SM adhesive was composed of two fitted peaks for primary amine (–NH2, 400.7 eV) and secondary amine (–NH–, 399.8 eV). With the introduction of DACS and DACS-HNTs@N, the SM-DACS and SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesives produced new fitting peaks at 398.6 and 398.8 eV, respectively, which were designated as tertiary amines (–N=), indicating the formation of Schiff base [58,59]. However, the –N= signal intensity of the SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive was stronger than that of the SM-DACS adhesive. This result suggested that more Schiff base reactions occurred in the adhesive system in the presence of HNTs@N, which was associated with the introduction of HNTs@N to bring a significant amount of active amino groups.

FTIR spectra were used to further investigate the interactions between organic and inorganic components in adhesives. All SM-based adhesives showed similar typical characteristic peaks (Fig. 4b). For the SM adhesive, the peak at 3397 cm−1 was attributed to the NH and OH groups [19]. The peak of CH stretching appeared near 2930 cm−1. The peaks at 1654 and 1541 cm−1 were attributed to amide I (C=O) and amide II (NH). The addition of CS introduced abundant amino groups, which could explain the enhancement of NH stretching (3422 cm−1). The incorporation of DACS reduced the NH stretching (3393 cm−1) and NH bending (1535 cm−1) in the SM-DACS adhesive. This was attributed to the reaction of the aldehyde groups of DACS with the amino groups of SM via Schiff base reaction [60]. This result can also be confirmed by the peak of CO bonds (1659 cm−1). The addition of HNTs or HNTs@N did not result in covalent cross-linking, at which point hydrogen bonding was the way to connect organic and inorganic materials. Compared to the SM-DACS, HNTs@N further reduced the NH stretching peak (3350 cm−1) and the CO shifted from 1659 to 1664 cm−1. These changes were attributed to the occurrence of Schiff base reactions between SM, DACS, and HNTs@N.

TG and DTG were used to characterize the pyrolytic properties of SM-based adhesives [61]. SM-based adhesives showed two obvious stages of weight loss from 30 to 600 °C (Fig. 4c). The first mass loss of the adhesive without TGA occurred from 30 to 180 °C, mainly due to the escape of moisture. The second mass loss occurred at 180–360 °C. This stage corresponded mainly to the breakage of hydrogen bonds in the adhesive, unstable chemical bonds, and covalent bonds such as CC, CO, and CN groups. The third mass loss occurred at 360–600 °C, which corresponded to the further cleavage of the protein backbone. Obviously, the addition of cross-linker TGA increased the residual rate and maximum degradation temperature of the adhesive, which was attributed to the ring-opening reaction between TGA and protein, thus increasing the degree of cross-linking of the adhesive to some extent. Compared to CM-CS, the maximum degradation temperature of SM-DACS was increased from 304 °C to 315 °C, which was caused by the formation of covalent Schiff bases, and the thermal stability of the adhesive was improved. The addition of inorganic HNTs@N material increased the adhesive residue rate, which was related to its structure. The maximum cleavage peak of SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive appeared at 339 °C, which was attributed to the double Schiff base of DACS with organic and inorganic materials that increased the number of covalent bonds. Especially, the SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive showed the highest mass fraction of 36.3 % at 600 °C, which was 13.2 % higher than that of the SM adhesive. This was attributed to the introduced HNTs@N with superior thermal stability and the formation of a denser polymer network through sufficient cross-linking and hydrogen bonding interactions between protein chains, DACS, and HNTs@N molecules.

XRD was used to characterize to measure the crystal structure of adhesives (Fig. 4d). In the XRD curve of the pure SM adhesive, the diffraction peaks with 2θ = 8.4° and 19.2° were attributed to the α-helical and β-sheet structure of soybean protein, respectively [62]. After incorporating the CS, HNTs and HNTs@N, the crystallinity of the obtained adhesives increased to different degrees, which was attributed to the lack of effective chemical linkage within the adhesive system, but only simple physical hydrogen bonding. In comparison with the SM and SM-CS adhesives, the XRD spectra of SM-DACS adhesive showed a significant decrease at 8.4° and 19.2°, which indicated that the addition of DACS broke the symmetry of protein molecular chains and reduced the crystallinity of the adhesives. The same trend occurred in the SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesives.

The mechanical performance of adhesive was the most crucial property. The shear strength of plywood was used to characterize the mechanical strength (Fig. 5a-b). The dry and wet shear strengths of the unmodified SM adhesive were 1.59 and 0.62 MPa, respectively. The latter failed to meet the Chinese national standards. The adhesives prepared by the addition of CS and HNTs individually failed to achieve the requirement because the lack of efficient covalent linkage cannot properly strengthen the cross-linking network of the adhesives. The addition of organic bio-crosslinker DACS and aminated inorganic nanotubes HNTs@N can simultaneously increase the dry and wet shear strength of SM-based adhesives. DACS molecular chains with abundant reactive aldehyde groups reacted with the amino group in SM via Schiff reaction. The formation of covalent bonds improved the degree of cross-linking of the adhesive, which increased the wet shear strength of SM-DACS to 1.18 MPa. Hydrogen bonding occurred between the active amino groups on the surface of HNTs@N and the polar groups on the SM. The amino groups also underwent an epoxy ring opening reaction with a little TGA. The simultaneous addition of inorganic aminated fillers and organic crosslinkers greatly increased the mechanical properties of the adhesive. The dry shear strength was 2.39 MPa and the wet shear strength was 1.53 MPa, which were increased by 50.3 % and 146.8 %, respectively.

The amount of DACS and HNTs@N added to the adhesive was optimized (Fig. 5c). The shear test of SM-DACS adhesives demonstrated an optimal DACS mass fraction of 10 wt%. The wet shear strength tests showed that the ternary SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive containing 2.5 % HNTs@N based on SM mass performed the highest mechanical performance. The wet shear strength of the sample was 1.53 MPa, which was 146.8 % and 29.7 % higher than that of the SM and SM-DACS adhesives, respectively. When the addition of HNTs@N was 1 %, it could not perform better to fill in the adhesive. However, when more than HNTs@N were introduced (>5 %), DACS was unable to provide sufficient binding sites. The excess Schiff covalent could disrupt the equilibrium of the cross-linked network and thus increased the brittleness of the adhesive layer, which would decrease the mechanical property of the adhesive.

The wet shear strength of different SM-based adhesives was compared with their crosslinker additions (Fig. 5d). The SMK-CPO adhesive was enhanced by keratin and calcium phosphate oligomers [63], the SP/M adhesive was modified by biomimetic organic-inorganic composites [64], the SM/BP adhesive was modified by the addition of epoxidized bark extract [65], the SPI/D/B adhesive was modified by the addition of a specially formulated cross-linking agent, the SBAM adhesive was enhanced by constructing a microcapsule cross-linking system [66], the MCF/LAQ@AC adhesive was modified by the addition of biomineralized cellulose nanocellulose through a supramolecular strategy. The adhesive prepared in this paper used the least crosslinker and possessed a comparatively high wet shear strength. This reduced production costs and simultaneously conformed to the sustainable and green development trends.

The organic-inorganic structures connected by Schiff base enhanced the water resistance of the SM-based adhesives. The water resistance of adhesives was characterized by residual rate and moisture absorption (Fig. 5e). The residual rate of the pure SM adhesives was 67.2 %. This poor water resistance was attributed to the numerous water-intolerant groups of proteins and polysaccharides in SM. The SM-DACS residue rate increased by 6.8 % compared with SM-CS, attributed to the formation of Schiff bases. Noteworthy, the residual rate of the SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive was 79.2 %. This decrease in moisture absorption of the adhesive confirmed the increase in the cross-linking degree. The dense cross-linked network prevented the intrusion of moisture.

To some extent, the strength of the bonding network can be reflected by the wood breakage rate (Fig. 5g). The wood breakage rate of the plywood prepared with SM adhesives was 5 %, while the addition of DACS increased the wood breakage rate of plywood to 72 %. Interestingly, the plywood prepared with SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive had a 95 % fracture rate. This result was consistent with the analysis of shear strength described above and proved the improved mechanical performance of the adhesive.

The enhancement mechanism of the mechanical strength of the adhesive was further investigated by observing the SEM of the dried SM-based adhesives. Many cracks appeared on the surface of the pure SM adhesive (Fig. 6a). Cracks reduced the interface interaction of adhesive-wood and gluing and made it easier for moisture to penetrate the adhesive layer, thus leading to low wet shear strength. The addition of CS reduced the number and size of cracks, which showed that CS was well-compatible with SM. The hydrogen bonding between CS and SM enhanced the cross-linking network of SM-CS adhesive to some extent, but the cracks remained. The cracks in SM-DACS adhesive were further reduced and gradually dispersed into many small cracks because the Schiff covalent and hydrogen bonds dispersed the internal stresses. Holes of different sizes appeared in the SM-HNTs@N adhesive. This indicated that the interaction of HNTs@N and the SM matrix was not sufficient to properly increase the degree of cross-linking. The SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive showed a highly dense cross-section with further reduction in the number and size of cracks and holes due to the uniform distribution of HNTs@N in the cracks of the adhesive, thus increasing the interfacial friction and interactions in the adhesive. DACS both acted as an SM crosslinker between SM and HNTs@N, and as a bridge between SM and HNTs@N. Thus, this organic-inorganic composite adhesive was characterized by a densely cross-linked structure.

Generally, the debonding work was positively correlated with the toughness of the cured SM based adhesives [67]. The adhesion work of the adhesives was obtained by calculating the integral of the force-distance curve (Fig. 6b). The adhesion work of pure SM adhesive was 103.5 mJ, which showed that the cured adhesive layer was very brittle, and the toughness was poor. In contrast, the adhesion work of the SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive increased by 276.5 % to 389.7 mJ and the strain of break increased from 0.46 mm to 0.77 mm. The enhancement of the adhesive cohesive strength can also be demonstrated by the morphological changes in the cured SM adhesive (Fig. 6c). The pure SM adhesive showed many large holes and cracks related to the inherent brittleness. However, the SM-CS adhesives showed larger cracks because the hydrogen bonding was weaker and less prone to breakage. With the introduction of DACS, the cracking of SM-DACS adhesives was reduced. This was because the DACS chain segments obtained by oxidation of sodium periodate became flexible compared to CS. In addition, the Schiff base reaction of –CHO and –NH2 enhanced the covalent linkages within the adhesive. The SM-HNTs@N adhesive showed small cracks, which was attributed to the filling effect of HNTs@N. The SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive showed the smoothest surface. This was due to the covalent and hydrogen bonds dispersing the internal stresses, which can effectively dissipate energy and improve the toughness of the adhesive. The significant increase in toughness contributed to the stress transfer when the cured adhesive layer was subjected to tension.

To evaluate the mildew resistance of SM-based adhesives, five SM-based adhesives were placed in sealed bags and then placed at room temperature conditions (25 °C). The changes in the surface of the adhesives and the possible changes in odor were observed at different times (Fig. 7a). All five different formulations of the freshly formulated adhesives reveal smooth surfaces. After 24 h, numerous molds were found on the SM and SM-HNTs@N adhesives surfaces, accompanied by foul odors. The SM-CS, SM-DACS, and SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesives were not affected by fungi or bacteria within 288 h and remained homogeneous in texture and odorless. After 360 h, slight changes appeared on the surface of the SM-CS, SM-DACS and SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesives; small numbers of molds were found. The favorable anti-mold property of SM-CS was determined by the reaction between the amino group on the CS molecular chain, the negatively charged cell membrane inside the fungus or bacteria, and the leakage of proteins and other components inside the microorganism, thus leading to inactivation. The difference was that the mold resistance of the SM-DACS and SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesives depended not only on the amino groups of DACS but also on the antibacterial properties of the Schiff base. In addition, the mold behavior of the fresh liquid adhesives was tested under confined conditions (30 °C and 95 % relative humidity). Compared to SM adhesive, the SM-DACS and SM-DACS-HNTs@N also showed better mold resistance (Fig. S1). The wet shear strengths of SM-based adhesives with different storage times (stored sealed at room temperature) were used to evaluate the mold resistance as well (Fig. 5f). The wet shear strength of the SM and SM-HNTs@N samples showed a faster rate of decrease and the pressed plywood could no longer be immersed in water at 63 °C for 3 h after 36 h of storage. The decreasing trend of the wet shear strength of the SM-CS, SM-DACS, and SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesives have been slowed down. After 60 h storage, the SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive still maintained the high strength. Fig. 7b shows the mold resistance of commercially available urea-formaldehyde resin and cured SM-based adhesives. Mold appeared on the surface of the urea-formaldehyde resin at 50 d due to the addition of flour. The mold trend of the cured SM-based adhesives was like the liquid adhesives and the adhesives with CS/DACS showed better mold resistance.

Plywood was susceptible to fungal infestation and mildew [68]. The improvement of mold resistance was further analyzed by observing the mold behavior of plywood prepared with commercially available urea-formaldehyde resins and different formulations of SM-based adhesives under high temperature and high humidity conditions (Fig. 7c). All plywood maintained a smooth surface for 14 d. mold appeared on the plywood prepared with SM and SM-HNTs@N adhesives at 21 d and more mold appeared in the following 20 d, attributed to a fungal attack of SM adhesives. Mold was found on the surface and sides of plywood prepared with SM-CS, SM-DACS, and SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesives at 40 d. This was attributed to mold on the veneer and adhesive. The plywood prepared with commercially available urea-formaldehyde resins showed the same trend, indicating that the addition of CS/DACS promoted the mold resistance of the plywood.

The raw material cost of SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesives was assessed in Table S1 and the cost of commonly used UF/MUF resin, PF resin, commercially available cross-linker polyamide-epichlorohydrin (PAE)-modified SM-based adhesive, 1,2,3-propanetriol diglycidyl ether (PTGE)-modified SM-based adhesive and SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive was assessed in Table S2. The cost of SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive was approximately 2673.5 RMB /Ton, which was lower than PF resin (4200 RMB /Ton) and commercially available SM adhesives (3200 RMB /Ton), which showed great potential for industrial production. In addition, compared to recently reported representative SM/SP based adhesives [20,68–71], the prepared SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive exhibited excellent overall performance, including higher dry shear strength, higher wet shear strength, lower crosslinker addition, lower cost, longer mold resistance time and increased toughness (Fig. 8 ). Based on the above-mentioned benefits, SM-DACS-HNTs@N provided the opportunity for the industrial application of SM-based adhesive, which is in line with the development concept of sustainable and renewable development. The modification of natural materials and organic-inorganic hybridization strategies provided viable solutions for the preparation of functional composites.

In this study, we have successfully developed SM-based adhesive with high strength, toughness, water resistance, mildew resistance, low cost, and low chemical addition by constructing a natural organic-inorganic hybrid structure in polymer through a Schiff base reaction and new energy dissipation mechanism. Tests conducted on the plywood showed that the dry and wet shear Strength and debonding power of SM-DACS-HNTs@N adhesive were 2.39 MPa, 1.53 MPa, and 389.7 mJ, which improved by 50.3 %, 146.8 %, and 276.5 %, respectively. The moisture uptake and residual rate tests showed that the water resistance of the adhesive was also improved. DACS and Schiff's base had good antimicrobial properties, which provided the adhesive with good mold resistance, extended the storage time of the adhesive, and the durability of the plywood. Compared to commercially available SM-PAE and SM-PTGE adhesives, SM-DACS-HNTs@N showed lower costs, providing a realistic basis for its industrial application. The synthesis and preparation process are simple and green. All raw materials were natural and inexpensive, in line with the concept of sustainable and renewable development. Thus, this research offered a viable solution for creating natural plant protein materials with desirable water resistance, strength, toughness, mold resistance, and economic befits. Also, the modification of natural materials and organic-inorganic hybridization strategy provided a feasible way to prepare functional composite materials.
